items.title: Pug Horton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 22, 1998
items.q: I think that Hamilton in bestowing this honorary doctorate on him have done a very wise thing.

ctx.x: Right. You seem to make a good pair. And I know over the twenty years you’ve had quite a significant hand in Bob’s career. Did you, when you first got into trying to further his career, was it a steep learning process for you, of how to negotiate contracts and how to open avenues? How to get him in other parts of the world that he hadn’t been in before?

No. Because tenacity is my middle name. And I felt when I got to know Bob better, that he was far more — he was deserving of far more than he’d actually achieved. When he was young he had a lot of acclaim with The Wildcats and with the bands that he had, and I think he went into a sort of period of what I thought was something semi-obscurity, which I thought was unfair, and I thought that we had to dig really fast in order to make up for lost time. And at that point I took on a lot of chores that I didn’t expect…

to me. I wrote four grants for him to the NEA and got them for him, because I felt that he certainly is passing on a legacy, just as one was passed on to him. I think that Hamilton in bestowing this honorary doctorate on him have done a very wise thing. I know they’ll never regret it. And so for me, life has always been hurdles. I love them. I think that it’s just something to do. I mean you don’t just look at it and say well what should we do, you get on with it. And I think that’s part of my north country…
